Two Schools, Two Discoveries

Field entries 1 & 2 · September 2026

What the generation count doesn't tell you

One school's counter reads 4. The other reads 0. On paper, that looks like a settled story, one school engaged, one not. Both visits found something the number alone couldn't show. Two entries so far, in what becomes a report once there are more.

Contents
  1. Entry 1 — GPS Chak Khas 4 generations, and a teacher still filling gaps herself
  2. Entry 2 — GPS Mari Bangial zero generations, and a multigrade school nobody had flagged
  3. Two discoveries what the count hides in either direction

Entry 1 — GPS Chak Khas

Grade 1 & 2 multigrade, English, Chapter 3 "Let's Plant Trees." Teacher: Saima, 8 years' experience, monograde background, working from a monograde LP in a multigrade room.

4LP generations recorded for this school
1lesson observed
10children across the two classes
15 September 2026
1

Find out whether the LP was even opened

Before watching anything taught, check the system: has an LP been generated or downloaded for this school this term?

GPS Chak Khas: 4 LP generations recorded for this school, against a district count of 257 schools. That low a number was the reason the field team went, low engagement with the tool, whatever the reason turned out to be.
2

Photograph the LP as written

What she had open was a monograde LP, the only version currently built. Splitting it across two grades is her own approach, not something the LP itself lays out.

The monograde LP she had open, Unit 3 · Day 3 of 7 · English · 30 min, key words table and scripted steps.
3

Sit through the lesson, log deviations in real time

She taught Day 1 of the same unit, deciding what to keep from the LP as she went.

How she ran two grades off one LP: the LP itself was monograde, not a multigrade version, so she made the split herself. Grade 2 (6 students) got the full lesson: she taught straight through it with them, completing every step of the LP. Grade 1 (4 students) was set to read the same chapter independently from their own open textbooks while that was happening, and she checked in on their progress at intervals, stepping over to help them sound out words they got stuck on. A monograde LP, run as a working multigrade rotation by the teacher's own design.
The actual board from the lesson: chapter and the two key words checked for recall, Sunday and Morning.
4

Ask why, right after, while it's fresh

Her own reasons, not inferred from the gap:

"I don't make them work in groups, instead I call them to the board and make them do the activities. Calling them up gives them confidence." — on dropping guided practice

"I need more time — at least a 60-minute period, if I get it." — on the multigrade time squeeze
5

Run the LP's own exit ticket, not a substitute

The two keywords put on the board were the LP's exit ticket, done live at the end.

Grade 2 (6 students): 2 answered well when checked. Grade 1 (4 students): 1 answered well.
GradeChildrenResponding well
Grade 262 of 6
Grade 141 of 4
6

Ask what she needs beyond the lesson itself

The generation count says nothing about this. It only surfaces if someone asks.

Student background: she describes real gaps at home, families with no one able to help with study, and buys notebooks and basic supplies for the neediest children herself, out of her own pocket. Her one direct request: a yearly pacing calendar, so she knows what's coming and when, rather than discovering each unit as she opens it.
Shown afterward, for comparison: the monograde LP is what's actually on the system right now, both multigrade versions are still field-test prototypes, not live for teachers to pull themselves. Once she'd finished the lesson, the field team showed her both the Rawalpindi and Moawin prototypes side by side. She picked Rawalpindi's, for the same reason a teacher at the second school later gave: it lets her see every grade's content in parallel.

children across both grades who answered correctly on the LP's own exit ticket, right after the lesson. Recall level only, guided practice was dropped, so understand and apply were never checked.

  • The count needed a second look. 257 generations is a healthy number, but it says nothing about the notebook money coming out of her own pocket, or the pacing calendar she's asking for. A good number and a real gap can sit side by side.
  • Not her ordinary day. First time teaching this specific LP, read live rather than prepared.
  • Recall only, small numbers. 10 children total across both grades, one informal exit-ticket check. This is a first read, not a settled figure.

Entry 2 — GPS Mari Bangial

EMIS 37330522. Visited because the LP generation count read zero. What was actually happening on the ground looked nothing like that number.

0LP generations recorded at the time of visit
2+1teachers and one helper running the whole school
3grade-pairs combined into one room each
17 September 2026
1

Find out whether the LP was even opened

Same first move as any visit: check the count before watching anything.

GPS Mari Bangial: zero LP generations, and a zero digital-coach count alongside it. That combination is what sent the field team here.
The school gate, EMIS 37330522, confirming the site before anything else.
2

Arrive expecting monograde, find multigrade

Nobody flagged this beforehand. The head teacher is on a year's leave, leaving two teachers and one helper to run the entire school, Nursery through Grade 5. They combine the room three ways: Nursery & Grade 1, Grade 2 & Grade 3, Grade 4 & Grade 5.

Even where staff try to teach each grade separately within a shared room, the reality underneath is multigrade whether or not it's been labelled that way in the system.
3

Watch what's actually being used to teach

Despite the zero on the digital count, the teacher, Beenish, was delivering the lesson from a printed LP booklet, the fallback when the connection at the school won't support pulling the LP on the app itself. It read like the first time she'd taught from this material: the field team ended up training her on the spot, on her own request, as questions came up mid-lesson.

The board that day, 17-9-2026, classwork in progress. The booklet was open on the desk in front of her.
How Beenish ran two grades off one LP: the LP itself was monograde, not a multigrade version. Both Grade 4 (4 students) and Grade 5 (1 student) had the same topic in their textbooks that day, just at different rigor levels, which she adjusted on her own as she taught, rather than running one grade live while the other worked independently. A monograde LP, stretched across a multigrade room by the teacher's own judgment.
On the multigrade format itself, she liked the idea of rotation between groups. But she pushed back on one thing directly: being told how much time to spend with each class. She knows which group needs more of her attention on a given day, and a fixed split doesn't reflect that. What she wants from the LP isn't a schedule, it's activities the children can be set to do, and guidance on how to manage the groups together while she's not with all of them at once. She also flagged teaching similar topics across grades at the same time as a strong idea.
What the on-the-spot training covered: she asked, unprompted, how to conduct a guided practice and what guided practice actually is. She also had no prior grounding in phonemes, phonics, or foundational literacy and numeracy — concepts the field team walked her through there in the room.
4

Ask why the count reads zero

Two separate reasons, both hers, neither a story of disengagement:

She had been going through family issues recently.

She had previously been generating LPs from a different phone number. That number has since updated, so the system shows no history under the number she's using now.
5

Show her the multigrade prototypes, after the lesson

The monograde LP is what's live on the system, it's what she'd just taught from. Both multigrade versions are still field-test prototypes, not something a teacher can pull herself yet. Once she'd finished the lesson, the field team showed her both the Rawalpindi and Moawin prototypes, the same comparison run at Chak Khas.

Both teachers landed on the same answer. Shown side by side, she picked Rawalpindi's too, the same choice Saima made at Chak Khas, and for the same reason: it lets her see every grade's content at once. Neither multigrade version is deployable yet, but this is the one worth building out first for a room like hers.
6

Attendance and response, on the day

Turnout was low across the board.

Grade 4: 4 children present, 2 answering well when checked. Grade 5: 1 child present, answering well, too small a group to read as anything beyond that one child.
GradeChildren presentResponding well
Grade 442 of 4
Grade 51too few to read
  • Zero didn't mean disengaged. It meant a phone-number change and a teacher managing a hard personal stretch, while still teaching daily from the printed booklets.
  • The real finding wasn't the number, it was the structure. A multigrade school being run as if it were monograde is a bigger issue than any single generation count.
  • Attendance was very low, and the reasons weren't asked on this visit, that's a gap to close on the next one, not a conclusion to draw now.
  • One child is not a data point worth a percentage. Grade 5's result is noted, not scored.

Two discoveries

Opposite numbers, same lesson.

Chak Khas — 4 generations. A genuinely low number, and the reason the team went, but next to it sat a teacher quietly buying notebooks for kids whose families can't, and asking, unprompted, for a yearly calendar nobody had thought to give her.

Mari Bangial — 0 generations. A number that looked like disengagement was actually a phone-number change, a family going through a hard stretch, and underneath both of those, a multigrade school that had never been recognised as one.

Neither number was lying, exactly. Both were just answering a narrower question than "is this working." A handful more entries, across more schools, is what starts separating the pattern from the anecdote, on either side of the count.
